{{short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Modular forms modulo ''p''}}
In [[mathematics]], [[modular form]]s are particular complex [[analytic function]]s on the [[upper half-plane]] of interest in [[complex analysis]] and [[number theory]]. When reduced [[Modular arithmetic|modulo a prime ''p'']], there is an analogous theory to the classical theory of complex modular forms and the [[p-adic modular form|''p''-adic theory of modular forms]].

==Reduction of modular forms modulo 2==
===Conditions to reduce modulo 2===
[[Modular form]]s are analytic functions, so they admit a [[Fourier series]]. As modular forms also satisfy a certain kind of [[functional equation]] with respect to the [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] of the [[modular group]], this Fourier series may be expressed in terms of <math>q=e^{2 \pi i z}</math>.
So if <math>f</math> is a modular form, then there are coefficients <math>c(n)</math> such that <math>f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} c(n)q^n</math>.
To reduce modulo 2, consider the subspace of modular forms with coefficients of the <math>q</math>-series being all integers (since [[complex number]]s, in general, may not be reduced modulo 2).
It is then possible to reduce all coefficients modulo 2, which will give a modular form modulo 2.

===Basis for modular forms modulo 2===
Modular forms are generated by <math>G_4</math> and <math>G_6</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last=Stein |first=William |date=2007 |title=Modular Forms, a Computational Approach |url=https://wstein.org/books/modform/modform/index.html |at=Theorem 2.17 |publisher=Graduate Studies in Mathematics |isbn=978-0-8218-3960-7}}</ref>
It is then possible to normalize <math>G_4</math> and <math>G_6</math> to <math>E_4</math> and <math>E_6</math>, having integers coefficients in their <math>q</math>-series.
This gives generators for modular forms, which may be reduced modulo 2.
Note the Miller basis has some interesting properties:<ref>{{cite book |last=Stein |first=William |date=2007 |title=Modular Forms, a Computational Approach |url=https://wstein.org/books/modform/modform/index.html |at=Lemma 2.20 |publisher=Graduate Studies in Mathematics |isbn=978-0-8218-3960-7}}</ref>
once reduced modulo 2, <math>E_4</math> and <math>E_6</math> are just <math>1</math>; that is, a trivial reduction.
To get a non-trivial reduction, one must use the modular discriminant <math>\Delta</math>.
Thus, modular forms are seen as polynomials of <math>E_4</math>,<math>E_6</math> and <math>\Delta</math> (over the complex <math>\mathbb{C}</math> in general, but seen over integers <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> for reduction), once reduced modulo 2, they become just polynomials of <math>\Delta</math> over <math>\mathbb{F}_2</math>.

===The modular discriminant modulo 2===
The modular discriminant is defined by an infinite product,
<math>
\Delta(q) = q \prod_{n=1}^\infty (1-q^n)^{24} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \tau(n)q^n,
</math>
where <math>\tau(n)</math> is the [[Ramanujan tau function]].
Results from Kolberg<ref>{{cite journal|last=Kolberg |first=O. |date=1962 |title=Congruences for Ramanujan's function <math>\tau (n)</math> |journal=Årbok for Universitetet i Bergen Matematisk-naturvitenskapelig Serie |issue=11 |mr=0158873}}</ref> and Jean-Pierre Serre<ref>{{cite book |last=Serre|first=Jean-Pierre |date=1973 |title=A course in arithmetic |publisher=Springer-Verlag, New York-Heidelberg |page=96 |isbn=978-1-4684-9884-4 }}</ref> demonstrate that, modulo 2, we have
<math> \Delta(q) \equiv \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} q^{(2m+1)^2} \bmod 2</math> i.e., the <math>q</math>-series of <math>\Delta</math> modulo 2 consists of <math>q</math> to powers of odd squares.

==Hecke operators modulo 2==
The action of the [[Hecke operator]]s is fundamental to understanding the structure of spaces of modular forms. It is therefore justified to try to reduce them modulo 2.

The Hecke operators for a modular form <math>f</math> are defined as follows:<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last=Serre|first=Jean-Pierre |date=1973 |title=A course in arithmetic |publisher=Springer-Verlag, New York-Heidelberg |page=100 |isbn=978-1-4684-9884-4 }}</ref>
<math>T_nf(z) = n^{2k-1}\sum_{a \geq 1,\, ad=n,\, 0 \leq b < d} d^{-2k}f \left( \frac{az+b}{d} \right)</math>
with <math>n \in \N</math>.

Hecke operators may be defined on the <math>q</math>-series as follows:<ref name="auto"/>
if <math>f(z) = \sum_{n \in \Z} c(n)q^n</math>, 
then <math>T_nf(z) = \sum_{m \in \Z} \gamma(m)q^m</math> 
with

: <math>\gamma(z) = \sum_{a | (n,m),\, a \geq 1} a^{2k-1} c\left( \frac{mn}{a^2} \right).</math>

Since modular forms were reduced using the <math>q</math>-series, it makes sense to use the <math>q</math>-series definition. The sum simplifies a lot for Hecke operators of primes (i.e. when <math>m</math> is prime): there are only two summands. This is very nice for reduction modulo 2, as the formula simplifies a lot.
With more than two summands, there would be many cancellations modulo 2, and the legitimacy of the process would be doubtable. Thus, Hecke operators modulo 2 are usually defined only for primes numbers.

With <math>f</math> a modular form modulo 2 with <math>q</math>-representation <math>f(q) = \sum_{n \in \N} c(n)q^n</math>, the Hecke operator <math>T_p</math> on <math>f</math> is defined by <math>\overline{T_p}|f(q) = \sum_{n \in \N} \gamma(n)q^n</math> where
: <math>
\gamma(n) = \begin{cases}
  c(np)        & \text{ if } p \nmid n \\
  c(np)+c(n/p) & \text{ if } p \mid  n
\end{cases} \quad \text{ and } p \text{ an odd prime}.
</math>

Hecke operators modulo 2 have the property of being nilpotent.
Finding their order of nilpotency is a problem solved by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]] and [[Jean-Louis Nicolas]] in a paper published in 2012:.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nicolas |first1=Jean-Louis |last2=Serre |first2=Jean-Pierre |date=2012 |title=Formes modulaires modulo 2: l'ordre de nilpotence des opérateurs de Hecke |journal= Comptes Rendus Mathématique|volume=350 |issue=7–8 |pages=343–348 |doi=10.1016/j.crma.2012.03.013 |arxiv=1204.1036 |bibcode=2012arXiv1204.1036N |s2cid=117824229 |issn=1631-073X }}</ref>

==The Hecke algebra modulo 2==
The [[Hecke algebra]] may also be reduced modulo 2.
It is defined to be the algebra generated by Hecke operators modulo 2, over <math>\mathbb{F}_2</math>.

Following Serre and Nicolas's notations,
<math>\mathcal{F} = \left\langle \Delta^k \mid k \text{ odd} \right\rangle</math>, i.e. <math>\mathcal{F} = \left\langle \Delta, \Delta^3, \Delta^5, \Delta^7, \Delta^9, \dots \right\rangle</math>.<ref name="auto1">{{cite journal |last1=Nicolas |first1=Jean-Louis |last2=Serre |first2=Jean-Pierre |date=2012 |title=Formes modulaires modulo 2: structure de l'algèbre de Hecke |journal= Comptes Rendus Mathématique|volume=350 |issue=9–10 |pages=449–454 |doi=10.1016/j.crma.2012.03.019 |arxiv=1204.1039 |bibcode=2012arXiv1204.1039N |s2cid=119720975 |issn=1631-073X }}</ref>
Writing <math>\mathcal{F}(n) = \left\langle \Delta, \Delta^3, \Delta^5, \dots, \Delta^{2n-1} \right\rangle</math> so that <math>\dim(\mathcal{F}(n)) = n</math>, define <math>A(n)</math> as the <math>\mathbb{F}_2</math>-subalgebra of <math>\text{End}\left(\mathcal{F}(n)\right)</math> given by <math>\mathbb{F}_2</math> and <math>T_p</math>.

That is, if <math>\mathfrak{m}(n) = \{T_{p_1} \cdot T_{p_2} \cdots T_{p_k} \mid p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k \in \mathbb{P}, k\geq 1\}</math> is a sub-vector-space of <math>\mathcal{F}</math>, we get <math>A(n) = \mathbb{F}_2 \oplus \mathfrak{m}(n)</math>.

Finally, define the Hecke algebra <math>A</math> as follows:
Since <math>\mathcal{F}(n) \subset \mathcal{F}(n+1)</math>, one can restrict elements of <math>A(n+1)</math> to <math>\mathcal{F}</math> to obtain an element of <math>A(n)</math>.
When considering the map <math>\phi_n: A(n+1) \to A(n)</math> as the restriction to <math>\mathcal{F}(n)</math>, then <math>\phi_n</math> is a homomorphism.
As <math>A(1)</math> is either identity or zero, <math>A(1) \cong \mathbb{F}_2</math>.
Therefore, the following chain is obtained:
<math>\dots \to A(n+1) \to A(n) \to A(n-1) \to \dots \to A(2) \to A(1) \cong \mathbb{F}_2</math>.
Then, define the Hecke algebra <math>A</math> to be the projective limit of the above <math>A(n)</math> as <math>n \to \infty</math>.
Explicitly, this means
<math>A = \varprojlim_{n \in \N} A(n) = \left\lbrace T_{p_1} \cdot T_{p_2} \cdots T_{p_k} | p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k \in \mathbb{P}, k\geq 0 \right\rbrace</math>.

The main property of the Hecke algebra <math>A</math> is that it is generated by series of <math>T_3</math> and <math>T_5</math>.<ref name="auto1"/>
That is:
<math>
A = \mathbb{F}_2\left[ T_p \mid p \in \mathbb{P} \right]
  = \mathbb{F}_2 \left[\left[ T_3, T_5 \right]\right]
</math>.

So for any prime <math>p \in \mathbb{P}</math>, it is possible to find coefficients <math>a_{ij}(p) \in \mathbb{F}_2</math> such that
<math>T_p = \sum_{i+j \geq 1} a_{ij}(p) T_3^iT_5^j</math>.
